newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Discount Bank offering in jeopardy.
newsitem.headline: Discount Bank offering in jeopardy.

text.p: Next week's Israel Discount Bank offering is in jeopardy after the Securities Authority said it wanted figures on the bank's fourth-quarter debt provision, a Discount spokeswoman said on Friday.

The spokeswoman said she did not know when the prospectus for the offering would be published but that it would not be on Friday. The propectus had been due to be published on Thursday before the authority asked for the additional information, which Discount said it did not yet have.

"The Securities Authority has demanded for the purposes of granting approval to provide it with exact quantitative data which is not currently available to the bank," Discount, referring to the debt provision and its impact on earnings, said in an announcement to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
Discount noted in the statement that the deadline for publishing a prospectus based on the bank's third-quarter results was February 28.
"We are investigating the possibilities of continuing contacts with the Securities Authority," Discount said.
After that date, the bank would have to wait until full-year 1996 earnings were published. The banks generally publish the full-year results in late March.

The planned offering by the government, which is part of its bank privatisation effort, is for 17 percent of Discount's equity in a package of shares and warrants worth approximately 630 million shekels at the bank's current market capitalisation.

The authority asked for more information on the debt provision after Discount informed it on Wednesday that the provision would "significantly" reduce fourth-quarter earnings, due to the bank's lending to the property development sector.
"The bank estimates that the fourth quarter of 1996 will require a significant increase of specific provisions for doubtful debts compared with the third quarter," the bank said.
Discount, Israel's third-largest commercial bank, is one of the banks whose shares were withdrawn from trading after the government bailed out sharesholders in the wake of the 1983 bank shares crash.
The government re-floated shares and warrants in the bank in March 1996. They were equal to 14.5 percent of equity.
